what: Griffith P. Taylor built a Meccano programmable crane robot (punched-tape controlled, five axes) that stacked blocks; published in Meccano Magazine, March 1938.

sources.title: Industrial robot
sources.quote: The earliest known industrial robot conforming to the ISO definition was completed by

note: Fits the ISO definition mechanically but is a hobby model that did no factory work, so it is weak as a demonstration of factory labour. Unimate prototype (c.1958-60) and Roselund/DeVilbiss spray-painting patents (1938-42) considered; could not fetch sources for them (only Wikipedia reachable).

what: First Unimate installed at GM Inland Fisher Guide plant, Ewing Township NJ, lifting hot die-cast parts.

sources.title: Unimate
sources.quote: which worked on a General Motors assembly line at the Inland Fisher Guide Plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, in 1961

sources.title: Unimation
sources.quote: In 1960, Devol personally sold the first Unimate robot, which was shipped in 1961 to General Motors.

note: Some sources (Automate.org, not fetchable here) say a prototype was installed at GM Trenton in 1959; unverified. DeVilbiss painting robot (1940s) has no verified deployment.

what: Unimation, called the world's first robotics company, shipped its first Unimate to General Motors.

sources.title: Unimation
sources.quote: Unimation was the world's first robotics company

sources.title: Unimation
sources.quote: In 1960, Devol personally sold the first Unimate robot, which was shipped in 1961 to General Motors.

note: First commercial robot sale/delivery. Founding date is inconsistent (Wikipedia says 1962; first pass said 1956). Mass-production and repair aspects of the definition not separately dated.

what: Larry Roberts's MIT PhD thesis 'Machine Perception of Three-Dimensional Solids' (block-world scene analysis from camera images).
note: Source supports the thesis and 1963 PhD, 'father of computer vision'; the quote does not itself describe the demo. Earlier pattern-recognition/photoelectric-eye work (1950s) not searched successfully. Navigation by vision (Shakey, 1966-72) is later.

what: Westinghouse's Elektro (built 1937-38) shown at the 1939 New York World's Fair; walked by voice command, spoke about 700 words, moved head and arms.

sources.title: Elektro
sources.quote: he could walk by voice command, speak about 700 words

sources.title: Elektro
sources.quote: Elektro was on exhibit at the 1939 New York World's Fair

note: Earlier than first-pass WABOT-1 (1973), but Elektro was largely remote-scripted and did not handle objects in the human sense; fit is loose. Eric (1928) and WABOT-1 pages could not be verified.

what: Fanuc's robot plant near Mount Fuji runs lights-out, robots building robots, unsupervised for up to 30 days.

sources.title: Lights out (manufacturing)
sources.quote: FANUC, a Japanese robotics company, has been a lights-out factory since 2001.

note: First pass cited a 1981 report of Fanuc unattended operation (16 hours a day); I could not verify it, so a much earlier event likely exists. Date here is the latest-source date only.

what: Research on electronic noses (Persaud and Dodd, Warwick, Nature 1982) began.

sources.title: Electronic nose
sources.quote: Since 1982, research has been conducted to develop technologies, commonly referred to as electronic noses

note: Quote supports only the 1982 start of e-nose research. Earlier tactile sensors for robots/prostheses (1960s-70s) and Moncrieff's 1961 mechanical odour sensor likely earlier but unverified.
